body:
Short answer: A touch screen kiosk for an event is a touch display on a floor stand or enclosure, running one locked-down app such as sign-in, a product catalog, lead capture, wayfinding or a game. Pick the form factor and size from the job, choose Android for simple web apps and Windows for heavier software, plan for the network failing, and test the full flow before doors open. If nobody needs to touch the screen, rent a regular TV instead.

[[IMAGE]]

This guide covers what to rent, what to run on it, and the setup details that decide whether an interactive touch screen display works all day or freezes at the first rush.

Touch screen kiosk vs touch display on a stand vs wall-mounted

The three options use similar screens. The difference is how the screen is held, how protected it is, and how guests approach it.

  • Touch screen kiosk — An enclosure or pedestal that hides the computer, cables and ports. It looks finished, resists tampering and suits public areas, lobbies and long show days.
  • Touch display on a stand — A commercial touch screen on a rolling or fixed floor stand. Flexible, quick to set up, easy to tilt or swap between portrait and landscape. Good for booths and short events.
  • Wall-mounted touch screen — Saves floor space and works well for wayfinding and schedules. It needs a solid wall or a freestanding frame, and the touch area must stay within reach.

Tables and tilted stands are worth a look for games and collaborative content, because people naturally gather around a screen they can lean over.

Portrait or landscape

Portrait feels like a kiosk. It fits a single person, takes less floor width and works well for forms, photo capture and wayfinding. Landscape suits catalogs, video and anything two people use at once. Decide orientation before content is designed, because a layout built for one rarely looks right on the other.

Screen size by use

Size should follow how close people stand and how many use it at once. These are typical ranges, not hard rules.

UseTypical sizeOrientationWhy
Sign-in and registration22–32 inPortrait or landscapeFast, simple form. Pair with a badge printer if needed.
Product catalog32–55 inLandscapeSpace for images, filters and detail views.
Photo and lead capture32–43 inPortraitCamera at eye level, guest framed head to waist.
Wayfinding and schedules43–55 inPortraitReadable from a few steps away; map plus search.
Games and group experiences55–86 inLandscapeBig enough for two or three people at once.

A larger screen draws more attention, but it also means more reaching. On a tall portrait screen, keep buttons in the middle band, not at the top edge.

Android, Windows or a web app in kiosk mode

Most commercial touch displays now come with Android or Windows built in, so you may not need a separate computer at all.

  • Android — Starts fast, runs web apps and simple native apps well, and is easy to lock to a single app. A good default for forms, catalogs and video.
  • Windows — Use it for desktop software, TouchDesigner or Unity builds, heavier 3D content, and USB devices like badge printers, scanners and card readers.
  • Web app in kiosk mode — A browser locked to one URL, full screen, with no address bar. Quick to update, but it depends on the network unless the app is built to work offline.

You can run your own app or have one built. Our team builds custom touch and interactive content in house, including TouchDesigner pieces and real-time 3D, through our interactive installations work.

Network and offline fallback

Venue Wi-Fi is the most common reason a touch screen rental fails on the day, and the first thing to plan for in any touchscreen kiosk rental. Hundreds of phones crowd the same channels, captive login pages block devices, and the connection drops at peak times.

  • Build for offline — Store entries on the device and sync later. Cache images, video and the catalog locally.
  • Use a dedicated network — A private event network, wired where possible, keeps kiosks off the guest Wi-Fi. See our event Wi-Fi rental in NYC.
  • Show a clear state — If the app is offline, it should still work and say so quietly to staff, not show an error to guests.

Lead capture and data privacy basics

Lead capture is one of the best uses of a kiosk, and the one with the most responsibility. Keep it simple and clear.

  • Ask for less — Name, email and one question beat a ten-field form. Every extra field costs entries.
  • Consent in plain words — Say what you will send and add an unticked opt-in box. Link a short privacy notice.
  • Clear the screen — Reset to the start after each entry and after a short idle timeout so the next guest never sees someone else's details.
  • Protect the data — Encrypt stored entries, export to your CRM securely, and wipe the device before it goes back.

ADA reach height and accessibility

Under typical ADA guidance, anything a guest has to touch should sit between about 15 and 48 inches above the floor, with clear floor space in front, typically 30 by 48 inches, for a wheelchair to pull up. Set the stand height with that in mind. Use large buttons, good contrast, readable text, and an alternative such as a QR code that opens the same form on a phone.

Cleaning and hygiene

Touch screens collect fingerprints fast. Bring a microfiber cloth and a cleaner approved for coated displays, and wipe between sessions. Put a small sign and hand sanitizer next to busy kiosks. Avoid spraying liquid directly on the screen or using harsh solvents.

Security: locking down the OS

An open kiosk is an invitation. Guests will swipe from the edges, long-press, and try to open a browser.

  • Single-app mode — Use Android kiosk mode or Windows assigned access so only your app can run.
  • Disable gestures and keys — Turn off edge swipes, notifications, system menus and on-screen keyboards you do not need.
  • Hide ports and power — Cover USB ports and the power button, and route cables inside the stand.
  • Auto-recover — Set the app to restart after a crash and the device to boot straight into it.

Testing before the event

Run the full flow on the actual hardware, on the actual network, at the actual height. Check touch accuracy at the corners, the idle reset, the offline mode, the export of leads, and a restart from power off. Give staff a one-page sheet with how to reset the kiosk and who to call. For the wider show list, see our AV checklist for trade show exhibitors.

TV rental for events: when you do not need touch

Not every screen needs to be interactive. For a looping brand video, a session schedule, a sponsor reel or a presenter's slides, a regular TV is the simpler choice. Large OLED TVs on floor stands or mounts give deep blacks and wide viewing angles, and a playback station handles content without a laptop. Transparent displays are another option when you want product to show through the image. Many events mix a few touch kiosks with several plain screens, and our display rentals cover both, along with TV stand rental and mounts.

Frequently asked questions

What size touch screen kiosk do I need for event registration?

For self check-in, a 22 to 32 inch screen at standing height is usually enough, since guests only type a name or scan a code. Go larger only if the screen also has to attract people from across the floor.

Can a touch screen kiosk work without Wi-Fi?

Yes, if the app is built for it. A good setup stores sign-ups on the device and syncs when the connection returns, so a network drop never stops guests from using the kiosk.

Should I use Android or Windows for an event kiosk?

Android is the simpler choice for web apps, forms and video playback. Windows is better when you need desktop software, a TouchDesigner or Unity build, or a USB device such as a badge printer or card reader.

What height should a touch screen kiosk be for accessibility?

Keep everything a guest has to touch between about 15 and 48 inches above the floor, which is the typical ADA reach range. Leave clear floor space in front so a wheelchair user can pull up, and avoid controls only at the very top of a tall portrait screen.

Do I need a touch screen, or will a regular TV do?

If the screen only plays a loop, shows a schedule or mirrors a presenter, a regular TV is the better and simpler choice. Pay for touch only when guests actually need to interact with the content.

How far ahead should I book a touch screen kiosk rental?

Book as early as you can when the kiosk runs a custom app, since the software needs time to build and test. Hardware only, running a web page or your existing app, needs less lead time but still benefits from a test day.
